The analysed sample is a white to faint pink, medium-grained (average groundmass grainsize ~1.5 mm), slightly porphyritic, leucocratic muscovite-biotite granite. K-feldspar (~35%; microcline) is the dominant feldspar. It forms scattered, subhedral to anhedral phenocrysts, up to ~1 cm long, as well as smaller anhedral grains in the groundmass. Quartz (~35%) is irregular to rounded and up to ~5 mm across. The quartz grains show evidence of extensive deformation-namely, highly undulose extinction and local subgrain development. These highly strained grains are a distinctive bluish grey colour in hand specimen. Plagioclase grains (~20%) are found mainly in the groundmass (where they form subhedral laths up to ~1.5 mm long), but also as sparse phenocrysts up to ~5 mm in length. They are variably zoned and slightly to extensively replaced by sericite. Biotite (~4%) is the dominant ferromagnesian mineral and is slightly more abundant than muscovite. The biotite grains (up to ~3 mm in length) have tabular and, locally, irregular habits. They are pleochroic from bright reddish brown (fox-red) to pale yellow (straw). Zircon (commonly surrounded by prominent dark brown to black pleochroic haloes), apatite, and, to a lesser extent, ilmenite are the most common inclusions. Muscovite (~3%) crystallised relatively late, mainly as aggregates of several small grains in interstices. Some biotite grains have also been partly replaced by muscovite around grain boundaries and along cleavage planes. Accessory minerals include zircon, apatite, ilmenite, and cassiterite? Sericite and chlorite are relatively common secondary minerals. Minor amounts of chlorite are present in most biotite grains, but a few have been extensively to completely replaced.

SAMPLE_DESCRIPTION: Chalcocite, bornite, chalcopyrite, and pyrite share common bedding and replacement textures, ranging from semi-massive accumulations, to disseminations, to very coarse blebs, and occasionally can form veins. Sulphides commonly mantle and or partially replace clasts in the diamictite. Chalcopyrite, bornite and chalcocite are commonly concentrated in sandy lenses and planar beds within the Ki1.1.1.2 siltstone-sandstone interbed of the basal diamictite. This appears to reflect a local permeability control on the distribution of mineralisation, and is also common in Zambian Ore Shale-hosted deposits. The footwall R4.2 (RFS) sandstone does not generally host significant hypogene mineralisation, as it is located below the redox boundary.

The sample is feldspar-phyric dacite. Highly altered feldspar minerals are suspected to be either K-feldspar or plagioclase. Individual phenocrysts are up to 8 mm in length, and are highly chloritic- to sericitic-altered, soft (easily scratched) and white in colour. The groundmass, only visible in thin section, is comprised of fine-grained quartz and feldspar. Altered feldspar phenocrysts show relict twinning consistent with plagioclase. Suspected pyroxenes and amphiboles are heavily altered to chlorite. Cracks and veins are filled with recrystallised quartz, carbonate and chlorite minerals. The Anthony deposit is a molybdenum-bearing porphyry system, which is hosted by a series of intrusive rocks into the Anakie Metamorphic Group. The deposit was discovered in 2007 by Zamia Minerals and is 70 km north-west of Clermont. The intrusive rocks, which do not crop out, are referred to informally as the Dead Horse Bore Complex in company reports (Daven and Doman, 2011; Doman and Daven, 2013). They are thought to be the source of the disseminated pyrite and molybdenite mineralisation at the deposit, thus determination of their crystallisation age may help constrain the age of mineralisation. ANTH02 is a composite sample of quarter core from the intervals 370-377.8 m and 385.1-391.5 m in drill hole RCD11A074, drilled for Zamia Minerals in February 2011. The intrusion sampled is thought to represent a mineralising phase and therefore provides a direct age constraint on mineralisation at Anthony. The sample selected from drill core is a cream to brown, strongly altered porphyritic biotite-hornblende monzogranite. In thin section the rock comprises abundant large relicts of former alkali feldspar and plagioclase phenocrysts now almost completely altered to sericite, altered biotite phenocrysts and rare altered hornblende. The groundmass appears recrystallised and comprises abundant sub-millimetre crystals of quartz and less abundant, muscovite and microcline.

The Overlander Granite forms several small elongate, sill-like plutons in the far NE of the Duchess 1:100 000 area. It is regarded as coeval with the Burstall Granite farther north, the Revenue Granite to the south, and the granitic component of the nearby Myubee Igneous Complex (e.g., Bultitude et al., 1978, 1982; Blake et al., 1984), and was included in the Burstall Suite by Budd et al. (2001). The granite is resistant to erosion in the area around the sample site and forms an extensively dissected plateau with abundant outcrop. The sample was collected from a low, blocky outcrop on the upper, western slope of a high ridge. Here, the granite is foliated, pale pink, fine- to medium-grained, leucocratic, K-feldspar rich, and is cut by quartz veins up to ca 30 cm thick (which were avoided during sampling). The granite is extensively deformed and partly recrystallised to fine-grained (0.3-0.5 mm) aggregates of quartz and microcline, with minor plagioclase and rare biotite and muscovite. These aggregates are interspersed with zones of much coarser (1-3 mm) relict grains of mainly microcline microperthite and quartz. Quartz shows highly undulose extinction and relict microcline grains have ragged outlines. Some larger, relict plagioclase grains show undulose extinction and/or bent twin planes. The recrystallised groundmass contains traces of muscovite, biotite and opaque oxide minerals. The granite is very leucocratic (mafic minerals << 5%). Accessory minerals include altered allanite and relatively common zircon. The Overlander Granite has attracted the interest of mineral exploration companies over the years as a possible source of the copper mineralisation in nearby country rocks (mainly Corella Formation). In addition, Hewlett (2013) reported IOCG-style alteration in some of these rocks. A sample of the granite was analysed to test the correlations of previous investigators and to provide age constraints on any genetically related mineralisation.

Sample 2804792/DPMI080 was collected from the depth interval 534.85-536.07 m in Exco Resources drillhole EMCDD094, drilled at Mount Colin Mine. The drillhole contains metasedimentary rocks (Corella Formation), granite, alteration, and high-grade copper mineralisation. The granite sampled from EMCDD094 is present in adjacent drillholes but is not exposed at the surface. The granite was selected for geochronology because it locally grades to crystallised hydrothermal phases, and appears intimately associated with mineralisation. The granite is heterogeneous and locally contains miarolitic cavities and xenoliths of highly altered Corella Formation rocks. The sample selected for geochronology is an altered, granophyric biotite alkali feldspar granite. In thin section, the sample is roughly even-grained to slightly porphyritic and comprises abundant K-feldspar as large subhedral grains with perthitic and graphic textures. Quartz is abundant as intergrowths and medium-sized crystals exhibiting undulose extinction. Plagioclase may have been present originally but is now completely altered. Relicts of mafic phases (possibly both biotite and amphibole) are present but sparse and now represented by chlorite, epidote and titanite.

This sample of an unnamed felsic dyke is from drillhole D86/71, drilled by Little River Goldfields N.L in 1986, and sampled at the GSNSW Londonderry core facility. This drillhole in the Dobroyde gold prospect intersected a quartz-veined, weathered, and propylitic-altered quartz and feldspar porphyritic rhyolite from 69.0 m to the end of the hole at 80.5 m (Elliot, 1989). The sample from interval 77.8-78.2 m is a brecciated and sericite-altered porphyritic rhyolite which contains sub angular, 2 mm plagioclase grains and 1-2 mm quartz phenocryst set in a fine-grained dark red groundmass. The red staining of the groundmass and plagioclase may be due to hematite alteration. This porphyritic rhyolite intrudes the unnamed andesite which hosts the Dobroyde gold deposit and is interpreted to pre-date mineralisation based on petrographic evidence, so an age will provide a maximum age constraint on the timing of mineralisation. In thin section the rock contains fractured plagioclase and quartz phenocrysts in a groundmass that has been recrystallised to a fine glass. The quartz crystals are rounded and approximately 0.5-0.8 mm in size. Some areas have undulose extinction indicating strain. Carbonate minerals are tan-brown with high birefringence and hatched carbonate twinning, and sometimes occurs as clay and sericite-altered glomerophyric clusters. Biotite is replaced by muscovite and sericite. The rock also contains opaque minerals. The rock has been sericite and carbonate altered, with veinlets throughout.
COMMENTS: 1/4 core from drillhole D86/71 drilled by Little River Goldfields N.L in 1986 and sampled at the GSNSW Londonderry core facility.

The quartz-feldspar porphyry consists of a very fine-grained greenish (altered) groundmass consisting of extremely fine-grained sericite (probably after feldspar) and quartz. The groundmass constitutes about 70% of the rock. Phenocrysts make up about 30% of the rock, of which about 60% are quartz, 35% are feldspar and 5% are muscovite. Quartz crystals are broken and partially resorbed, ranging from 0.1 mm to about 5 mm in length. They contain blebs and embayments of sericitised matrix. Arrowhead shaped terminations indicate quench crystallisation driven by strong undercooling. Rare quartz grains contain tiny tourmaline inclusions. Feldspar phenocrysts are tabular to sub-tabular and are up to about 2 mm long. They are strongly sericitised and iron oxide-corroded and are probably after alkali feldspar (rather than plagioclase). Muscovite (after biotite) forms iron oxide-corroded platy grains to about 1 mm. Clasts of country rock up to at least 4 cm long occur within the porphyry and consist of crenulated quartz-mica schist typical of Girilambone Group metasedimentary rocks.
